name: ATTINY9-TS8R
title: ATtiny4/5/9/10 8-bit AVR microcontrollers, 512/1024 bytes Flash, 32 bytes SRAM, 6-pin SOT23 and 8-pad UDFN
summary: ATtiny4, ATtiny5, ATtiny9 and ATtiny10 are 8-bit AVR RISC microcontrollers in a 6-pin SOT23 or 8-pad 2 x 2 mm UDFN, with 512 or 1024 bytes of Flash, 32 bytes of SRAM and four I/O lines. They run from 1.8 V to 5.5 V at up to 12 MHz, from a calibrated 8 MHz RC oscillator, a 128 kHz oscillator or an external clock, and carry a 16-bit timer with two PWM outputs, an analog comparator, a watchdog and a VCC level monitor; ATtiny5 and ATtiny10 add a 4-channel 8-bit ADC. Programming is external only, through the 3-wire TPI at 5 V. ATTINY10-TSHR is the 1024-byte ADC part in SOT23-6 for -40 to 85 °C.

Top marking x is the die revision. The bottom marking reads zHzzz on -40 to 85 °C parts and z8zzz on -40 to 125 °C parts.
Packages are Pb-free and halide-free with NiPdAu lead finish. The -40 to 85 °C parts are also offered as bare wafers.

circuits.title: In-system programming through TPI
circuits.description: A programmer header carries +5 V, ground and the three TPI lines (RESET, TPIDATA, TPICLK) straight to PB3, PB0 and PB1. The application shares those three pins, each through its own series resistor, and also takes VCC and PB2 directly. NVM programming works only with VCC at 5 V; series resistors are one way to protect application parts that cannot take 5 V.

operation.text: Four parts share one die design and pinout: ATtiny4 and ATtiny5 have 512 bytes of Flash, ATtiny9 and ATtiny10 have 1024 bytes. ATtiny5 and ATtiny10 add the 4-channel 8-bit ADC. All have 32 bytes of SRAM, four I/O lines, a 16-bit timer with two PWM outputs, an analog comparator, a watchdog and a VCC level monitor. Each part identifies itself by a three-byte signature.

AVR 8-bit RISC with 54 instructions, most executing in one clock, giving close to 1 MIPS per MHz (12 MIPS at 12 MHz). The register file has 16 registers, numbered R16 to R31; R26 to R31 pair up as the X, Y and Z pointers. The program counter is 9 bits wide. The status register is not saved automatically on interrupt entry.
The stack lives in SRAM and grows downwards; the stack pointer must point above 0x40. PUSH and POP move it by one, a call, interrupt, RET or RETI by two.

Flash is 256 or 512 words of 16 bits with at least 10,000 write/erase cycles. The CPU cannot write Flash; it reads it through the data space starting at 0x4000. I/O registers occupy 0x0000-0x003F (IN/OUT reach all 64; SBI/CBI/SBIS/SBIC work on 0x00-0x1F) and SRAM 0x0040-0x005F. LDS/STS reach 0x0040-0x00BF. SRAM access takes two CPU clocks. Reading NVM through the data space stalls the CPU one clock.
Retention: the projected failure rate stays well under 1 ppm for 20 years at 85 °C, and for 100 years at 25 °C.

Three main clock sources: the calibrated internal 8 MHz RC oscillator, an external clock on CLKI, or the internal 128 kHz oscillator, chosen by CLKMS1:0 in CLKMSR. Switching is glitch free and can be done at run time. The factory calibration byte is loaded into OSCCAL at every reset; OSCCAL 0x00 is the lowest frequency, 0xFF the highest. The 128 kHz oscillator always clocks the watchdog and the reset time-out.

The main clock passes through a prescaler set by CLKPSR, dividing by 1 to 256. After any reset the 8 MHz oscillator divided by 8 (1 MHz) runs the part. If the source is faster than VCC allows, software must choose enough division. Prescaler changes are glitch free and never pass through a frequency above both the old and new settings.
CLKMSR, CLKPSR and WDTCSR are changed only by first writing 0xD8 to CCP; the target register must then be written within four instructions, during which interrupts are held off.

When the reset source is released the part counts a 64 ms reset delay on the 128 kHz oscillator (the supply itself is not watched), then 6 cycles of oscillator start-up, then 21 clocks to load calibration and configuration from NVM. From power-down only the 6 oscillator cycles are counted; from idle, ADC noise reduction or standby the oscillator is already running.

SE in SMCR plus a SLEEP instruction enters the mode chosen by SM2:0. Idle stops the CPU and NVM clocks only. ADC noise reduction also stops clkI/O and starts an ADC conversion. Power-down stops the oscillator; only a watchdog event, an INT0 level interrupt or a pin change wakes the part. Standby is power-down with the oscillator left running for a fast wake-up. A wake-up adds four clocks before the interrupt routine runs, and register and SRAM contents survive.

PRR bits PRTIM0 and PRADC stop the clock to the timer and the ADC, freezing their state and blocking register access. The ADC must be disabled before it is shut down, and while it is shut down the comparator cannot use the ADC multiplexer.

Turn off the analog comparator in idle when it is not needed (it is off automatically in power-down); disable the ADC before any sleep, since it stays on otherwise and its next conversion is an extended one; turn off the watchdog when unused, as it runs in every sleep mode. Do not let pins drive resistive loads. Floating inputs or inputs near VCC/2 draw excess current in the input buffer; set DIDR0 for pins used as analog inputs. In power-down and standby the input buffers are clamped except on pins enabled as interrupts.

Three sources: power-on reset, a low level on RESET longer than tRST, and watchdog time-out. Port pins go to their reset state as soon as a reset source becomes active, with no clock needed. The vector at 0x0000 must be an RJMP to the reset routine. RSTFLR records which source caused the reset (PORF, EXTRF, WDRF).

The POR circuit holds the part in reset while VCC is under its threshold and starts the delay counter once VCC rises past it; reset reasserts immediately if VCC falls back. POR only works if the supply has first fallen below VPOA, and needs a rising slope of at least 0.01 V/ms.

A low level on RESET for longer than tRST resets the part even with no clock. On the rising edge, once the pin passes VRST, the part restarts after tTOUT. External reset is ignored during the power-on delay count; after power-on, reset is stretched only if RESET is still low when that count ends. RESET can be disabled by the RSTDISBL configuration bit, making PB3 a weak I/O pin.

The VLM compares VCC with one of four levels set by VLM2:0 in VLMCSR. VLM1L and VLM1H give a power-on reset below the level, held as long as VCC stays low, which resets the part earlier on a falling supply than POR alone. VLM2 and VLM3 set the VLMF flag and can raise an interrupt; the flag clears when VCC rises back above the level or the level is changed. The monitor draws current; it can be switched off or run in bursts, but it needs its settling time before a result is valid.

The watchdog runs from the 128 kHz oscillator with time-outs from 16 ms to 8 s (WDP3:0). It can reset the part, raise an interrupt (useful for waking from power-down), or raise an interrupt first and reset on the next time-out. WDR restarts the count. With WDTON unprogrammed the watchdog starts off and disabling it needs the CCP sequence; with WDTON programmed it is always on and only the time-out can be changed, again through CCP. WDE stays set while WDRF is set.

Eleven vectors from 0x0000; the lower the address, the higher the priority. Entering an interrupt clears the global I bit; RETI sets it again. Response takes at least four clocks, plus four more from sleep; the return takes four. The instruction after SEI always runs before a pending interrupt. Flag-type interrupts are remembered while disabled; level-type interrupts fire only while the condition lasts.

INT0 (on PB2) triggers on low level, any change, falling or rising edge. Edge detection needs the I/O clock; the low level and the PCINT3..0 pin-change interrupts are detected asynchronously and can wake the part from any sleep mode. Both fire even if the pin is an output. A level used to wake from power-down must be held until the start-up completes, or the part wakes without taking the interrupt. Edge pulses longer than one clock are guaranteed to be caught.

Port B has four pins with symmetrical drive strong enough for LEDs, individually switchable pull-ups (PUEB) and protection diodes to VCC and ground. DDRB sets direction, PORTB the output level, and writing a one to PINB toggles PORTB. Pin reads pass a synchronizer adding ½ to 1½ clocks of delay; reading back a value just written needs a NOP. Pins are tri-stated during reset. With BBMB set in PORTCR, turning a pin into an output inserts one clock of tri-state (break-before-make).

Give unused pins a defined level, simplest by enabling the internal pull-up (off during reset; use an external resistor if reset current matters). Tying a pin straight to VCC or GND risks a large current if it is ever set as an output.
Programming the CKOUT configuration bit puts the system clock on PB2, overriding PORTB2 and DDB2.

A 16-bit timer with two double-buffered compare units (OC0A on PB0, OC0B on PB1), one input capture unit (ICP0 on PB1, or the comparator output) with a 4-sample noise canceler, and four interrupts (TOV0, OCF0A, OCF0B, ICF0). Clocks: the I/O clock divided by 1, 8, 64, 256 or 1024, or the T0 pin on either edge. Modes: normal, CTC, fast PWM, phase correct PWM, and phase-and-frequency correct PWM, at 8, 9, 10 bits or with TOP from ICR0 or OCR0A. Its 16-bit registers need the high-byte-first access sequence.

Compares AIN0 (PB0, positive) with AIN1 (PB1, negative); ACO goes high when AIN0 is higher, 1-2 clocks after synchronisation. It can interrupt on toggle, rising or falling output and can trigger the timer's input capture (ACIC). ACD turns it off. Disable its interrupt before changing ACD or ACIS1:0. Use the pins as inputs with pull-ups off.

8-bit successive approximation ADC with a 4-input multiplexer on PB0-PB3, single ended to ground, with VCC as the only reference; inputs above VCC read 0xFF. It needs a 50-200 kHz clock for full resolution, made by the ADPS prescaler from the system clock. A normal conversion takes 13 ADC clocks, the first after enabling 25. Conversions start from ADSC, free running, or a rising edge of a chosen interrupt flag. ADC supply range is 2.5 V to 5.5 V. Clear PRADC and set ADEN before use; ADEN off draws no current.

MUX bits are buffered and latched when a conversion starts; change them before starting, or one ADC clock after setting ADSC. In free running mode the conversion already under way when the channel changes still uses the old channel.

The sample-and-hold sees a 14 pF capacitance through 1 to 100 kΩ. Sources of about 10 kΩ or less settle within the sampling time; higher impedances need longer. Content above fADC/2 should be filtered out first.

Keep analog tracks short, over an analog ground plane and away from fast digital lines; do not switch port outputs during a conversion; put bypass capacitors close to VCC and GND. ADC noise reduction mode, or idle, converts with the CPU stopped: enable the ADC complete interrupt, select single conversion, and sleep.

All non-volatile memory is programmed externally through the 3-wire Tiny Programming Interface: RESET as enable, TPICLK as clock, TPIDATA as bidirectional data. VCC must be 5 V. To enter, apply 5 V, wait tTOUT and pull RESET low for the whole session (or hold 12 V on RESET if RSTDISBL is programmed), wait tRST, then hold TPIDATA high for 16 TPICLK cycles. Frames are 1 start bit, 8 data bits LSB first, even parity and 2 stop bits. Two BREAK characters resynchronise the link. After the 64-bit SKEY key, poll NVMEN in TPISR before issuing NVM commands.

Flash holds four sections: code, configuration (one configuration byte with CKOUT, WDTON and RSTDISBL), signature and calibration; signature and calibration are read-only. The application can read all of it but cannot write it. Two lock bits give three modes. Configuration bits latch at reset or when leaving programming mode, survive chip erase, and are locked once NVLB1 is programmed. NVMBSY in NVMCSR shows a programming operation in progress.
The QTouch library supports one capacitive touch channel.

On all die revisions, programming the lock bits to a mode equal to or lower than the present one corrupts one word of Flash at a random location; the workaround is never to write the present or a lower lock mode. Die revision D (ATtiny4/5/9) and C-D (ATtiny10) meet ESD HBM (ESD STM 5.1) 1000 V.
